BRENT spot prices have risen to the highest for more than a month in a sign oil exports from the Middle East remain severely disrupted despite efforts to re-open the Strait of Hormuz. Dated Brent prices for one week ahead have climbed over $100 per barrel for the first time since late July and before that early June. Physical prices are rising even faster than futures and the backwardation is steepening – all indications the market is short of physical barrels despite efforts to shuttle crude through the Strait or bypass it entirely by redirecting crude flows through the Red Sea:

#Agriculture:  The @UNFAO Food Price Index rose 1.9% in August, a third consecutive monthly gain, while the year-to-date increase remains a moderate 2.5%. All commodity groups recorded higher prices, led by sugar (+11.9% m/m, +7% y/y), dairy (+2.3% m/m, -19% y/y) and grains (+2.2% m/m, +10.9% y/y).

On the sugar surge, the FAO highlighted growing concerns over the 2026/27 global supply outlook. Hot and dry weather has reduced EU sugar beet yield forecasts, while El Niño-related conditions are threatening production across key Asian producers. Lower output in Brazil’s Center-South region and India’s announcement of duty-free raw sugar imports added to the tightening outlook.

International cereal prices also rose across all major grains in August, supported by strong demand, weather-related concerns over US and EU crop yields, robust feed and ethanol demand, and continued uncertainty over Black Sea exports.

Vegetable oils rose just 0.6% in August but remain the biggest contributor to food price gains over the past year, up 17.2%. Higher palm and soy oil prices outweighed weakness in sunflower and rapeseed oils, with palm supported by strong import demand and El Niño-related production concerns in Southeast Asia.

Energy scarcity is powering commodities towards a record weekly close. Crude and refined fuels lead as supply risks stay elevated, while gold rebounds and agriculture cools after four strong weeks. This week’s Commodity Weekly looks at the key drivers behind the moves.  https://t.co/lWp3KFiIeH via @saxobank

Europe heads into winter with a thinner energy buffer. Low gas storage, constrained Qatari LNG supply and growing reliance on weather-dependent renewables leave less room for error. Yet rising US LNG supply, lower gas demand and potentially milder El Niño conditions offer important offsets.
 
The key risk is the combination: low storage + cold weather + weak wind/hydro + continued Qatari disruption.

Commodities
Oil: Crude trades steady after a three-session rally of around 9%, with WTI at USD 91.50 and Brent at USD 95.50. The US-Iran conflict around the Strait of Hormuz continues to keep supply risks and the geopolitical risk premium elevated. Brent has risen almost 60% this year, while refined products such as diesel have seen even steeper gains amid the Middle East conflict and Russia-Ukraine war. OPEC+ ministers meet on Sunday to set production targets.

Metals: Gold extended its rebound, rising as much as 2.9% on Thursday to above USD 4,500 an ounce, its biggest intraday jump since 19 August, supported by a weaker dollar and Waller’s remarks. Spot trades around USD 4,470 this morning. The largest bullion-backed gold fund recorded a USD 1.41 billion inflow, its largest since 16 January, while the senior gold miner fund rose 3.95% and silver 2.51%. In addition, central bank demand remains an important structural support. Following Waller’s comments, there is little doubt that next week’s August CPI print could have an outsized impact on market risk sentiment and where gold goes next. Key resistance is the 200-day moving average at USD 4,534.

The BCOM Total Return Index is heading for a weekly gain of around 2%, lifting its year-to-date advance to 33.6% and putting it on course for a record weekly closing high. Energy has done most of the heavy lifting, surging 6.3%, while agriculture trades softer following four weeks of strong gains that lifted the BCOM Agriculture Index by 12.6%. An end-of-week rebound across precious metals has left the sector near unchanged on the week, while industrial metals have recorded a small gain.
